content.overview: Section 61 BNS codifies the substantive law and punishment for Criminal Conspiracy, consolidating former Sections 120A and 120B IPC into a single unified section within Chapter IV. It defines conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act or a lawful act by illegal means. Where the agreement is to commit an offence, the agreement itself constitutes the completed offence without requiring any overt act. Sub-section (2) prescribes identical punishment to abetment for serious offences (two years plus, life, or death). Proof operates through the statutory agency rule under Section 8 BSA, with strict post-arrest admissibility cutoffs established in Navjot Sandhu.

content.study:
I. LEGISLATIVE REORGANIZATION & DUAL CONSOLIDATION
Section 61 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) is situated in Chapter IV ("Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt", Sections 45 to 62). In the colonial code, criminal conspiracy was unnaturally divided into two disparate provisions introduced late in 1913: Section 120A (substantive definition) and Section 120B (punishment). Parliament consolidated both provisions into Section 61 BNS, creating an integrated, comprehensive code for inchoate conspiratorial liability.

II. STATUTORY SCHEME & ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS
Section 61 provides:
"(1) When two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done—
(a) an illegal act; or
(b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy:
Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof.
Explanation.—It is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object.
(2) Whoever is a party to a criminal conspiracy,—
(a) to commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years or upwards, shall, where no express provision is made in this Sanhita for the punishment of such a conspiracy, be punished in the same manner as if he had abetted such offence;
(b) other than a criminal conspiracy to commit an offence punishable as aforesaid shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding six months, or with fine or with both."

Essential Ingredients:
1. Plurality of Persons: There must be at least two persons; a person cannot conspire with oneself.
2. Agreement (Consensus ad Idem): An agreement to do or cause to be done either an illegal act or a lawful act by illegal means.
3. The Proviso Gateway (Overt Act Requirement):
   - Agreement to Commit an Offence: The bare agreement constitutes the completed offence of criminal conspiracy; no overt act or execution is necessary.
   - Agreement to Commit Non-Penal Illegal Act: Where the object is an illegal act not amounting to an offence (e.g. a civil tort or breach of contract), an overt act in pursuance of the agreement by at least one party is mandatory.

III. JURISPRUDENTIAL FOUNDATIONS & LEADING AUTHORITIES
1. The Agreement as the Actus Reus:
   - In State of Tamil Nadu through Superintendent of Police, CBI/SIT v. Nalini & Ors. (1999) 5 SCC 253 (Rajiv Gandhi assassination case) and Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration) (1988) 3 SCC 609, the Supreme Court held that the essence of criminal conspiracy is the unlawful agreement. The crime is complete the moment the agreement is formed, regardless of whether the substantive crime is executed or frustrated.
2. Circumstantial Proof & Secrecy of Conspiracies:
   - In State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu @ Afsan Guru (2005) 11 SCC 600 (Parliament attack case) and Yogesh @ Sachin Jagdish Joshi v. State of Maharashtra (2008) 10 SCC 394, the Supreme Court recognized that conspiracies are hatched in privacy and darkness. Direct evidence of an explicit pact is rarely available. The agreement must be inferred from the cumulative conduct of the parties, surrounding circumstances, commonality of purpose, and concerted movement.
   - However, mere association, friendship, or knowledge of another's criminal inclination does not establish a meeting of minds.

IV. EVIDENTIARY SPECIAL RULE: SECTION 8 BSA (OLD S. 10 IEA)
The prosecution of conspiracy is uniquely governed by the statutory rule of agency codified in Section 8 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA):
1. Prima Facie Threshold:
   - Before Section 8 BSA can be invoked, the prosecution must establish a reasonable ground to believe that two or more persons have conspired together (prima facie case of conspiracy).
2. The Principle of Mutual Agency:
   - Once the threshold is met, anything said, done, or written by any one co-conspirator in reference to their common intention, after the time when such intention was first entertained by any of them, is a relevant fact against each co-conspirator to prove the conspiracy and complicity.
3. The Post-Termination Cutoff (Navjot Sandhu Limitation):
   - In Sardar Sardul Singh Caveeshar v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1965 SC 682 and Navjot Sandhu (2005), the Supreme Court ruled that Section 8 BSA applies strictly while the conspiracy is alive and ongoing. The moment the conspiracy terminates (either through success, abandonment, or arrest of the conspirator), any subsequent statement or confession made by one accused is inadmissible against co-accused under Section 8 BSA.

V. DISTINCTION BETWEEN CONSPIRACY, COMMON INTENTION & ABETMENT
1. Criminal Conspiracy (Section 61 BNS) vs Common Intention (Section 3(5) BNS):
   - Conspiracy is an independent substantive offence; common intention is merely a rule of evidence and attribution.
   - Conspiracy requires no overt act when the object is an offence; Section 3(5) requires active physical or supportive participation in the criminal act.
   - An accused may be convicted of conspiracy under Section 61 even if acquitted of the substantive offence, whereas Section 3(5) collapses if the substantive offence is not proved.
2. Criminal Conspiracy vs Abetment by Conspiracy (Section 45 Clause 2 BNS):
   - Under Section 45 Clause (2) BNS, abetment by conspiracy requires that an act or illegal omission must take place in pursuance of that conspiracy; under Section 61 BNS, the mere agreement to commit an offence is punishable without any act.

sections.heading: Legislative Architecture & Consolidation of Former Sections 120A and 120B IPC
sections.body:
Section 61 BNS consolidates the definition (former s. 120A IPC) and sentencing framework (former s. 120B IPC) into a single provision in Chapter IV.
Codifies criminal conspiracy as an inchoate offence, punishing the agreement prior to and independent of actual execution.
Sub-section (1) defines the two limbs: agreement to commit an illegal act, or a lawful act by illegal means.
The Explanation clarifies that it is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object or merely incidental.

sections.heading: The Proviso: Agreement to Commit an Offence vs Non-Penal Illegal Acts
sections.body:
Agreement to commit an offence: The bare agreement is the complete actus reus; no overt act is required.
Agreement to do non-penal illegal acts (civil torts, breach of legal duty): An overt act in pursuance of the agreement is mandatory under the statutory Proviso.
The Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. Nalini (1999) affirmed that consensus ad idem to commit a crime completes the offence.
A conspirator who joins the conspiracy after its formation is equally liable from the moment of joining.

sections.heading: Sentencing Architecture under Section 61(2) BNS
sections.body:
Section 61(2)(a): Conspiracy to commit serious offences (punishable with death, life imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment of 2+ years) is punished as if the conspirator had abetted the offence.
Section 61(2)(b): Conspiracy to commit any other minor offence is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.
Where an express provision penalizes conspiracy for a specific offence (e.g. waging war under s. 148 BNS), the specific provision overrides Section 61(2).
Conspiracy charges may run concurrently or consecutively with substantive completed offences.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Proof (BSA s. 8), Digital Evidence & Post-Arrest Admissions
sections.body:
Section 8 BSA enacts the doctrine of mutual agency: acts and statements of one conspirator bind all during the subsistence of the conspiracy.
The threshold condition: Prosecution must first establish reasonable grounds to believe a conspiracy exists before invoking Section 8 BSA.
Navjot Sandhu (2005) limitation: Statements made after arrest or after the conspiracy has ended are inadmissible under Section 8 BSA against co-accused.
Digital trails: Encrypted messages, call detail records (CDRs), and tower locations must be authenticated under Section 63(4) BSA.

sections.heading: Distinction from Section 3(5) BNS, Chamber Practice & Section 531 Transition
sections.body:
Conspiracy is an independent substantive offence; Section 3(5) is an evidentiary rule requiring an actual criminal act.
Acquittal of substantive charge does not bar conviction for conspiracy if the agreement is independently proved.
Defense advocacy: Establish mere casual association, absence of consensus ad idem, and exclusion of post-arrest co-accused statements.
Section 531(2)(a) BNSS transition: Use IPC Section 120B for conspiracies entered prior to 1 July 2024; Section 61 BNS for post-commencement pacts.

provisions.title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

examples.title: Agreement to Commit Murder — Completed Offence without Overt Act
examples.body: A and B meet in a private room and agree to assassinate politician P. They finalize the execution date and procure unregistered SIM cards. Before any weapon can be purchased or any attack launched, police intercept intelligence inputs, raid the hideout, and seize written murder plans detailing P’s security routes. A and B argue that because no physical attack took place, no offence was committed. Under Section 61(1) BNS, where the agreement is to commit an offence, the bare agreement constitutes completed criminal conspiracy. A and B are guilty under Section 61(2)(a) BNS and liable to punishment as abettors of murder.

examples.title: Agreement to Commit Civil Wrong — Proviso Requiring Overt Act
examples.body: Two businessmen X and Y agree to breach an exclusive supply contract with company C to drive down C’s market share (a civil wrong / tort, not a penal offence). They take no further steps and never implement the plan. Because the subject matter of the agreement is not an offence, the Proviso to Section 61(1) BNS applies, requiring an overt act besides the agreement. In the absence of an overt act in pursuance thereof, no criminal conspiracy is made out.

hypotheticals.question: As Senior Counsel appearing for M2 and M3, evaluate the admissibility of M1’s custodial confession under Section 8 BSA in light of State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu and assess whether the charge under Section 61 BNS can be sustained.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. The Cutoff Principle under Section 8 BSA (Navjot Sandhu Doctrine):
   - Under Section 8 BSA (old s. 10 IEA), things said or done by a conspirator are admissible against co-conspirators only if said or done "in reference to their common intention" during the currency of the conspiracy.
   - In Navjot Sandhu (2005) and Sardar Sardul Singh Caveeshar (1965), the Supreme Court held that once a conspirator is arrested, the conspiracy terminates as far as that conspirator is concerned. A post-arrest confession to the police is a narrative of past events, NOT an act done in furtherance or reference to the ongoing common intention.
   - Therefore, M1’s post-arrest custodial statement is entirely inadmissible against M2 and M3 under Section 8 BSA.
2. Evidentiary Value of Telegram Group Membership:
   - Mere presence in a digital chat group or passive membership without active participation or demonstrative consensus does not establish the meeting of minds required for Section 61 BNS (Yogesh @ Sachin Jagdish Joshi v. State of Maharashtra).
3. Requirement of Independent Corroboration:
   - The prosecution must independently establish financial transactions by M2 or cartographic contributions by M3 through verified electronic records under Section 63 BSA. In the absence of such independent proof, the charge under Section 61 BNS fails.

distinctions.title: Section 61 BNS (Criminal Conspiracy) vs Section 3(5) BNS (Common Intention)

rows.left: Independent substantive inchoate offence punishable on its own
rows.right: Rule of evidence and constructive attribution of liability; not an offence

rows.left: No overt act required where agreement is to commit an offence
rows.right: Active physical or supportive participation in the criminal act is essential

rows.left: Conviction can stand even if substantive offence fails or is aborted
rows.right: Collapses if the underlying substantive criminal act is not proved

distinctions.title: Section 61 BNS (Conspiracy) vs Section 45(2) BNS (Abetment by Conspiracy)

rows.left: Bare agreement to commit an offence constitutes the completed crime
rows.right: Requires that an act or illegal omission must take place in pursuance of the conspiracy

rows.left: Comprehensive self-standing provision in Chapter IV
rows.right: One of the three statutory modes of abetting an offence under Section 45

misconceptions.trap: Believing that an overt act is always necessary to constitute criminal conspiracy under Section 61 BNS.
misconceptions.correction: The Proviso to Section 61(1) BNS makes an express exception: an agreement to commit an offence requires NO overt act; the bare agreement is the complete offence. An overt act is required only where the agreement is to commit non-penal illegal acts.

misconceptions.trap: Relying on a co-accused’s post-arrest confession under Section 8 BSA to prove conspiracy.
misconceptions.correction: The Supreme Court in State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (2005) held that Section 8 BSA applies strictly while the conspiracy is ongoing. Post-arrest statements made to police are narratives of past events and are inadmissible against co-conspirators under Section 8 BSA.

misconceptions.trap: Citing Section 120A or 120B IPC in charge-sheets or arguments for post-1 July 2024 offences.
misconceptions.correction: Under the BNS, Sections 120A and 120B IPC are merged into Section 61 BNS. Citing IPC numbers for current offences violates statutory mandate; IPC is strictly historical concordance.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Senior Counsel Legal Assessment: Scope, Ingredients and Proof of Section 61 BNS
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. STATUTORY ARCHITECTURE & GENESIS
Section 61 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) consolidates the definition (former s. 120A IPC) and sentencing framework (former s. 120B IPC) into a single unified provision in Chapter IV ("Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt").

II. ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS
To secure a conviction under Section 61 BNS, the prosecution must establish:
1. Plurality: Agreement between two or more persons;
2. Object: To do or cause to be done an illegal act, or a lawful act by illegal means;
3. Execution Status:
   - If the agreement is to commit an offence: no overt act is required; the agreement itself is the crime.
   - If the agreement is to commit a non-penal illegal act: an overt act in pursuance thereof is mandatory under the Proviso.

III. SENTENCING TIERS UNDER SECTION 61(2)
- Serious Offences (death, life, or 2+ years RI): Punished in the same manner as if the accused had abetted the offence.
- Minor Offences: Imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.

IV. EVIDENTIARY REGIME & BSA SECTION 8
Conspiracy is proved primarily by circumstantial inference from coordinated conduct. Under Section 8 BSA, acts and declarations of co-conspirators are admissible against all, subject to the Navjot Sandhu limitation excluding post-arrest admissions.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Appellate Written Submissions: Exclusion of Post-Arrest Confessions and Inadequacy of Conspiracy Evidence
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
MAY IT PLEASE YOUR LORDSHIPS:

1. LOCUS OF THE CHALLENGE:
The appellant stands convicted under Section 61(2)(a) BNS and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment. It is submitted that the conviction is vitiated by reliance on legally inadmissible evidence.

2. INADMISSIBILITY OF POST-ARREST CONFESSION UNDER SECTION 8 BSA (NAVJOT SANDHU DOCTRINE):
(a) The sole piece of evidence connecting the appellant to the alleged conspiracy is the custodial confession of co-accused Accused No. 1 (Ex. P-14) recorded after his arrest.
(b) In State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu @ Afsan Guru (2005) 11 SCC 600, the Hon'ble Supreme Court authoritatively laid down that Section 8 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (old s. 10 IEA) operates on the principle of agency during the subsistence of the conspiracy. The moment a conspirator is arrested, the agency terminates.
(c) Post-arrest statements made by a co-accused to the police or judicial authorities are mere ex-post-facto narratives of past occurrences and cannot be received in evidence against co-conspirators under Section 8 BSA.

3. MERE ASSOCIATION DOES NOT CONSTITUTE CONSPIRACY (KEHAR SINGH & NALINI):
(a) Apart from the inadmissible confession, the prosecution has proved only that the appellant shared a meal with Accused No. 1 and had telephone contact.
(b) In Kehar Singh v. State (1988) 3 SCC 609 and State of Tamil Nadu v. Nalini (1999) 5 SCC 253, the Supreme Court ruled that mere association, acquaintance, or proximity is not evidence of conspiracy. There must be affirmative evidence establishing consensus ad idem and a meeting of minds.

4. PRAYER:
There being no legally admissible evidence establishing that the appellant entered into a conspiratorial agreement under Section 61 BNS, the appeal must be allowed and the appellant acquitted.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Comprehensive appellate submissions establishing the strict exclusion of post-arrest co-accused confessions under Section 8 BSA and applying the Navjot Sandhu and Nalini standards.

cases.name: State of Tamil Nadu through Superintendent of Police, CBI/SIT v. Nalini
cases.holding: The Rajiv Gandhi assassination appeals where the Supreme Court settled the doctrine of criminal conspiracy: the unlawful agreement is the very nucleus of the offence; once the agreement to commit a crime is proved, no overt act is necessary. A conspirator is liable for all acts done in furtherance of the common design.

cases.name: State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu @ Afsan Guru
cases.holding: The Parliament attack decision establishing the definitive limitation on Section 8 BSA (old s. 10 IEA): statements made by a conspirator after arrest are narratives of past events and cannot be admitted against co-conspirators because agency terminates upon arrest.

cases.name: Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration)
cases.holding: The Indira Gandhi assassination case holding that conspiracies are hatched in privacy and secrecy, requiring proof by circumstantial evidence, but mere association, friendship, or family ties cannot substitute for proof of agreement.

cases.name: Yogesh @ Sachin Jagdish Joshi v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: Reaffirmed that to frame a charge or convict for criminal conspiracy, the prosecution must show a meeting of minds (consensus ad idem) to do an illegal act; suspicion and conjectures cannot take the place of legal proof.

examTips: Always cite Section 61 BNS as the consolidated provision replacing both Section 120A (definition) and Section 120B (punishment) IPC.
Remember the Proviso: an agreement to commit an offence requires NO overt act; an agreement to do non-penal illegal acts requires an overt act.
Under Section 8 BSA, acts and statements of one conspirator bind all, but post-arrest confessions are strictly excluded (Navjot Sandhu).
Conspiracy is a separate substantive offence; an accused can be convicted under Section 61 even if the substantive offence is aborted or fails.
Under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, cite IPC Section 120B for conspiracies formed prior to 1 July 2024 and Section 61 BNS for post-commencement pacts.

examFrameworks.question: Structured Chamber Brief: Analyzing Liability under Section 61 BNS
steps: Verify plurality of actors (at least two persons).
Identify whether the object is an offence or a non-penal illegal act.
Apply the Proviso: determine whether an overt act is necessary and proved.
Evaluate circumstantial evidence of consensus ad idem (meetings, calls, fund transfers).
Examine admissibility of co-conspirator evidence under Section 8 BSA (rule out post-arrest statements).
Determine sentencing classification under Section 61(2)(a) or (b) BNS.

examFrameworks.question: Appellate Submissions: Challenging Criminal Conspiracy Conviction
steps: Demonstrate that the prosecution evidence proves mere association, not agreement.
Exclude co-accused post-arrest statements under Section 8 BSA and Navjot Sandhu.
Expose absence of independent corroboration under Section 63 BSA for electronic evidence.
Argue that suspicion cannot substitute for consensus ad idem (Yogesh Joshi).
Pray for acquittal under Section 61 BNS.

answerSkeleton: Introduction — Section 61 BNS, Chapter IV ("Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt"), consolidating IPC ss. 120A and 120B.
Essential Ingredients — Plurality (2+ persons), agreement (illegal act or illegal means), Proviso (no overt act needed for offence).
Punishment Architecture — Section 61(2)(a) (punished as abettor for serious crimes) and 61(2)(b) (up to 6 months for minor crimes).
Evidentiary Mechanism — Section 8 BSA mutual agency; Navjot Sandhu cutoff excluding post-arrest custodial statements.
Key Landmark Ratios — Nalini (agreement as crime), Kehar Singh (secrecy & circumstantial proof), Yogesh Joshi (consensus ad idem).
Distinctions & Transition — Distinct from Section 3(5) BNS and Section 45(2) BNS; BNSS s. 531 transitional rule.
revisionPoints: For offences, the bare agreement constitutes the completed crime without any overt act.
For non-offences, an overt act is mandatory under the Proviso.
Section 8 BSA allows acts of one conspirator to be used against all, but NOT after arrest (Navjot Sandhu).
Conspiracy is an independent offence, unlike common intention under Section 3(5).
